rationale: B wins because it respects the limits of the facts while still finding pressable stories. “Figma puts its AI code tool behind a new $25 seat” turns the disclosed price into a real buyer-budget angle, while A’s “Post-Adobe, Figma's First Major Launch Is a Bet That Designers Can Ship Production Code” smuggles in two unsupported claims: first-major status and production quality. A has bones, but B is less likely to get the founder embarrassed in a reporter’s inbox.
gaps_in_A: “first major product announcement as a fully independent company” is not in the update. The fact supplied is only that the launch follows the Adobe acquisition collapse.
“That's a different company than Adobe would have built” is a counterfactual with no evidence. That is analyst cosplay unless Figma or a credible third party says it.
“Post-Adobe, Figma's First Major Launch Is a Bet That Designers Can Ship Production Code” overclaims output quality. The set later admits the production-versus-prototype question is unresolved.
“Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io” may be useful context, but those competitors were not supplied. In a fact-bound exercise, that is decoration pretending to be evidence.
gaps_in_B: “faster work, fewer hours billed for it” invents labor economics. The update says layouts from prompts, not designer hours disappearing.
“it lands on 4 million desks” turns a user-count claim into implied deployment. Four million users is reach, not proof the assistant reaches or changes every user’s workflow.
“That silence is part of the story” may be true, but only if an executive will engage. Otherwise “no IPO timing disclosed” is context, not a capital-markets hook.
“moving the design tool into the developer's toolchain” is slightly ahead of the facts. Export capability is not the same as developer adoption.
